extracted.intended_audience: educated lay readers and skeptics interested in natural philosophy (astronomy) and theology
extracted.subtask_description: Using observational astronomy and natural-philosophical reasoning (tides, parallax, telescopic observations, planetary motion) to argue for theological conclusions and to explain celestial phenomena to skeptical readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental account of tides (moon-related observations)
rubrics_metrics.description: This is experimentally true, that the Waters  the deep and free Seas ... rise, and swell up to the Places, or about those Places where the Moon is vertical, just as if they were driven thitherward by Weight, or attracted or pressed by some other power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical criterion: observe that waters rise on the side where the Moon is vertical and similarly on the opposite side; note customary expressions that water rises when the Moon passes the meridian and falls when it goes away. Also observe that highest water is often about three hours after the Moon has been in the meridian (see Newton). Cite Kepler, Newton, Gregory, Whiston, Varenius for further reading. Acknowledge alternative accounts (e.g., Descartes) and that while causes may be debated, the experimental fact of swelling near lunar meridian is given as basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two tidal bulges/protuberances model
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Earth were covered all round with Water, it would appear Oval, by reason of the Swelling of the watry Surfaces on each Side; and these two Protuberances of Water or Mountains ... move continually round about the Earth, if they be not obstructed by Land, Shoals or otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this mental model to reason about global tides: two opposing water protuberances track the Moon, producing high tides on both near and far sides. Note obstructions (land, shoals) alter local manifestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for choosing between Copernican and Tychonic systems
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two Systems of the Heavenly Bodies ... The first seems to be the most convenient with respect to the annual Course of the Firmament, and is by many taken to be the true one, on account of its Simplicity: 'Tis that which we wont to ascribe to Copernicus ... The Second System bears the Name of Tycho Brahe ... seems in relation to the Planets to be nothing else but the former a little varied ... and for no other Reason than because Copernicus supposes the Earth to move about the Sun, and so it seems to contradict Scriptures, from which Tycho and his Followers make a Scruple of departing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two evaluative dimensions are offered for choosing a cosmological model: (1) simplicity and convenience of explanation (favours Copernicus); (2) agreement with Scripture (favours Tycho). The text presents these as legitimate criteria and notes that some combine features of both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parallax measurements to determine stellar distances / Earth's motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of inquiring into this distance with greater Certainty (if the Event had been favourable) has been since some Years set on foot by Messieurs Flamsteed and Hook, who thought that they could deduce from their Experiments, that the Diameter of the Earth's Way about the Sun (according to Copernicus) made some Alteration of Sight ... in proportion as the Parallax ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallax is presented as the key observational test for Earth's motion and for stellar distances; attempts by Flamsteed, Hooke, Cassini are cited. Guidance: apply precise observations across Earth's orbit to detect relative shift; recognize that failure to detect parallax (with instruments of the time) leaves distances and Earth's motion unresolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Huygens' assumptive method for estimating star distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Huygens ... supposes that a Star (at least one of the first Magnitude, such as Sirius, or the Great Dog-Star) is as big as the Sun; from whence he infers, that the Distance of the Stars from the Earth is ... many times greater than that of the Sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicitly acknowledged hypothesis: assume a star's true diameter equals the Sun's to derive distance from apparent size. The text marks this as speculative and without certain foundation; use cautiously and label as hypothetical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational limitation: stars appear as points — apparent diameters and magnitude undeterminable
rubrics_metrics.description: The best Telescopes that are made, can only represent the said Stars as so many Points of Needles, and without Breadth, insomuch that we can't discover any Measure of the apparent Diameters thereof by the Help of those Instruments; so that from the Impossibility of observing the Parallax, and especially the apparent Diameter, we are entirely disabled from determining the Magnitude of those Stars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat inability to resolve stellar discs with contemporary telescopes as a limitation—do not claim precise sizes or distances. Use parallax or other robust methods before inferring magnitudes; recognize that instrument resolution imposes epistemic bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increasing telescope power increases observable star count (innumerability conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Help of the [telescope], in the only Constellation of Orion ... more Stars ... show themselves, ... so that according to the Remarks ... by the Help of the same, ... more Stars are ... that the Number of the Stars is not to be counted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical guidance: improved instruments reveal previously unseen stars (Milky Way as many small stars, Magellanic Clouds resolved), implying practical impossibility of enumerating all stars. Use telescopic surveys to revise counts and caution against claims of finite totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and recording of novae and variable stars as observational facts
rubrics_metrics.description: That which is ... these Alterations among the fixed Stars; that some new ones appear, others that have been seen disappear; and a third forth show the same being sometimes with more and another time with a lesser Lustre ... In the Year 1604 ... several others may be found in Gregory, Lib. II. Sect. 30.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating stellar permanence, include records of historical novae and changes in magnitude; consult catalogs (Tycho, Hevelius, Mercator) and Transactions for specific cases. Treat variability as established observational phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for estimating planetary diameters and proportions (Huygens' comparative figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Huygens ... draw their magnitudes in a particular Figure in proportion to that of the Sun ... From his Observations we find the Diameter of the Sun ... 110 times greater than that of the Moon; 308 --- that of Mercury; 84 --- than that of Venus; 166 --- than that of Mars; 8558 --- than that of Jupiter; 43775 --- than that of Saturn ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proportional drawings and telescopic/observational data to estimate planetary diameters relative to Sun and Earth. Apply these ratios to infer volumes and comparative sizes; reference Huygens, 'Automata Planet.' and tables for numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computing planetary orbital velocities from distance and period (circumference/period method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute the Velocity: take the Diameter of the orbit (proportional to Earth-Sun distance), compute circumference, and divide by orbital period; example: Venus' circumference gives 43,982 Earth diameters in its period, compare to bullet distances to conclude Venus moves 146 times faster than a Cannon-bullet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: assume circular orbit, compute circumference = pi * diameter (use rational approximations if needed), divide by period to get linear speed; to give intuition, compare to known terrestrial speeds (e.g., cannon-bullet). Be explicit about assumptions (circularity, adopted Earth-Sun unit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating satellite orbital speeds and relative velocities (Cassini's moon example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose ... the nearest of Jupiter's Moons is distant from it 25 Diameters; one Day, eighteen Hours ... the whole Diameter of the said Revolution will be 57 ... the nearest Moon runs in one Day in its Way about Jupiter 201 Diameters of the Earth; and Jupiter ... runs 73 Diameters in its Orbit about the Sun in the said Space of a Day; that this Moon runs in its Orbis about thrice as fast as Jupiter itself, and consequently, a great deal above 100 times faster than a Cannon-Bullet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply same circumference/period method at planetary satellite scale; compute relative speeds by comparing satellite orbital path length per unit time to planetary orbital speed; compare with terrestrial benchmarks to illustrate magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical estimate of forces required to move planets (mass × velocity reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who understand Mechanics know, that by multiplying the Mass of two Bodies; each of them by its Velocity, the Proportion of the Powers that move them may be learned ... comparing Earth and Jupiter, Jupiter's force (mass × velocity) is computed to be many hundreds of thousands of times greater than that which moves the Earth with the same velocity as a Cannon-bullet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To estimate required force/strength: take proportional masses (from volume ratios inferred via diameters) and multiply by linear velocities to get comparative 'force' magnitudes; note assumptions about equal densities and acknowledge density differences could adjust numbers but not the qualitative conclusion of vastly greater forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theological argumentative use of astronomical incomprehensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: I have oftentimes most seriously reflected upon this Impossibility of determining the Magnitude and Distance of the Stars as an Effect of the adorable Wisdom of their Great Creator ... He therefore thought it necessary to make them immemutable, and to put them out of the Reach of all human Endeavour ... that those who despise him might be forced ... to confess a Power to be ... without Bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method of argument: employ empirical limits (undeterminable stellar sizes/distances, immense magnitudes, astonishing planetary motions) as philosophical/theological premises to argue for divine wisdom and greatness. Use observational humility as rhetorical device when addressing skeptics.
